title: Examples show the format
subtitle: Few-shot: three good examples beat a paragraph of rules
mission: Aurora’s support wants every ticket to have a subject in the format [Category] summary (#order). Instead of explaining the format, show the model examples. Find out how many are enough and why examples that are all alike become a habit.

predict.question: the prompt only says "write the subject of this email", with no examples. Does the model answer in the [Category] summary (#order) format?

options.free: No: writes free text, a different way each time
options.format: Yes: it already comes out in the format
options.error: Errors out, the format is missing

feedback.right: right: nobody told it the format, so the model picks one. With examples it copies the pattern without you describing it.
feedback.wrong: with neither an example nor a description, the model writes free text; there’s no error, just an answer the system can’t read. The examples are the specification.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run with 0 examples and look at the answer.

coach.ui: guess noted. Set "Examples" to 0 and run; then to 3.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run subject --examples 0 and then --examples 3.

tryNext.ui: Now the password email, which has no order number. With varied examples the subject comes out without the (#…): the example without a number taught that.
tryNext.cmd: Run subject "I can’t change my portal password: the email link never arrives." and see that it doesn’t invent a number.

why.simples:
Explaining a format in words is hard; showing it is easy. You give the model a few solved "email → subject" pairs and it continues the pattern, like seeing three rows of a filled spreadsheet and completing the fourth.
The risk: if the examples all look alike, it learns the habit too (every subject becomes "Billing").
why.dev:
Few-shot means putting input → output pairs in the prompt. Anthropic’s docs recommend 3 to 5 examples that are relevant (like the real use), diverse (covering edge cases so the model doesn’t pick up an unintended pattern) and wrapped in tags like <example>, so the model can tell them from instructions.
Examples steer format, tone and structure very reliably, but don’t guarantee it: for a strict output contract, combine with structured output (next lesson). Examples also cost tokens on every call.
why.especialista:
Each example is in-context training data: order may matter (there are reports that the last ones weigh more; test in your case), class proportions bias the output (five "Billing" examples push the answer to "Billing") and an error in one example gets copied. Treat examples like code: review, version and run the test set at every change.
When examples pile up, select them by similarity to the input (dynamic few-shot, using the same vector search as RAG) or, with volume and stability, move to fine-tuning. Here the model is simulated: real behavior varies by model and prompt, and only evaluation tells what works.

steps: Gather 5 real emails (without personal data) of one kind of ticket and hand-write the ideal subject for each, in the format your system expects.
Build the prompt with a short instruction and 3 of those pairs inside <examples> tags, each pair inside <example>. Test the other 2 emails.
Repeat with 3 pairs from a single category and compare the categories returned.
recipe.ok: with varied examples, the 2 test emails come out in the right format and category; with single-category examples, at least one comes out with the examples’ category.
